t.1.219.2: Deer and buffaloes by the hundreds, and birds as well, fled in every direction in great alarm, and so too did other kinds of creatures.
t.1.219.1: Then, terrified by the falling of the mountain, the dwellers of Khāṇḍava, the Dānavas, Rākṣasas and Nāgas, the hyenas, bears and other forest creatures, elephants in rut, tigers, lions and maned lions as well,
t.1.219.4: Janārdana hurled his discus, blazing with his own splendour; by it those lowly creatures, together with the Dānavas and night-roamers, were all cut down by the hundreds and in an instant fell into the fire.
t.1.219.5: There the Rākṣasas were seen, torn apart by Kṛṣṇa's discus, smeared with fat and blood, like clouds at twilight.
t.1.219.3: Gazing upon that forest fire and upon the two Kṛṣṇas with their weapons raised, they became as if terrified by the sound of the portentous roar.
t.1.219.6: Slaying piśācas, birds, nāgas and beasts too by the thousands, Vārṣṇeya moved about there like Death itself, O Bhārata.
t.1.219.7: For each time that discus of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of foes, was hurled, it killed many creatures and came back to his hand again and again.
t.1.219.8: And as he was thus slaying all creatures, O Bhārata, the form of him who is the self of all beings then became exceedingly fierce.
t.1.219.9: Of all the gods and Dānavas assembled together, not one became the conqueror of Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava in battle.
t.1.219.10: But when the gods, because of the might of those two, were unable to save that forest or to quench its fire, they then turned their faces away.
t.1.219.11: And Śatakratu, seeing the hosts of the gods turned away from the fight, stood still, pleased, praising Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava.
t.1.219.12: But when the gods had turned back, a bodiless voice, with a very deep and resounding tone, spoke, addressing Śatakratu.
t.1.219.13: Your friend Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents, was not present at the time of the burning of Khāṇḍava, for he had gone to Kurukṣetra.
t.1.219.14: Vāsudeva and Arjuna, standing arrayed in this battle, cannot be conquered by you, O Śakra; heed these words of mine.
t.1.219.16: These two cannot be conquered in battle, unassailable and unvanquished as they are, not even by all the worlds together, for they are the ancient seers, the most excellent of ṛṣis.
t.1.219.15: These two are the gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa, renowned in heaven; you too know well of what valor and of what prowess they are.
t.1.219.17: These two are most worthy of worship even by all the Suras and Asuras, together with the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, men, Kiṃnaras and Pannagas.
t.1.219.18: Therefore, Vāsava, you should go away from here together with the gods, and recognize this destruction of the Khāṇḍava as ordained by fate.
t.1.219.19: Having heard these words, the lord of the immortals thought, "This is true," and, casting off his anger and indignation, he then set out for heaven.
t.1.219.20: Seeing that great-souled one set out, O king, the dwellers of heaven swiftly followed Śatakratu, all together.
t.1.219.21: Then, seeing the king of the gods departing together with the gods, the two heroes Vāsudeva and Arjuna roared a lion's roar.
t.1.219.22: When the king of the gods had departed, O king, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, delighted, then once more set the forest ablaze without misgiving.
t.1.219.23: Like the wind scattering the clouds, Arjuna, having routed the gods, blasted with volleys of arrows the creatures dwelling in the Khāṇḍava forest.
t.1.219.25: There in battle, even the mighty beings were unable even to look upon Arjuna, whose arrows never miss; how then would they wage battle against him?
t.1.219.24: And no creature could escape from there, cut to pieces by the arrows of Savyasācin as he shot.
t.1.219.26: He pierced one with a hundred arrows, and a hundred with a single arrow; lifeless, they fell into the fire as if struck down by Kāla himself.
t.1.219.27: They found no refuge on the rugged riverbanks, nor in the abodes of the ancestors and the gods; there too a burning heat arose.
t.1.219.28: Thousands of hosts of creatures, in their distress, raised a great clamour; the elephants cried out, and so too did the beasts and birds. At that sound the fish that dwell in the Gaṅgā and the ocean trembled with fear.
t.1.219.29: For no one is able even to look upon the mighty-armed Arjuna, nor upon Kṛṣṇa of great strength; how much less, then, to fight them?
t.1.219.31: Their heads and bodies shattered by the force of the discus, those huge-bodied ones, their lives gone, fell into the mouth of the blazing Vasuretas.
t.1.219.30: And whatever Rākṣasas, Dānavas and Nāgas, driven onto the one narrow path, came rushing out from there, Hari slew them all with his discus.
t.1.219.32: Fanned and fed by floods of flesh and blood and by streams of fat, that fire, rising up into the sky, was seen to be smokeless.
t.1.219.34: Having obtained that nectar made ready by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, the Fire-god Hutāśana became delighted and sated, and attained supreme contentment.
t.1.219.33: With blazing eyes and blazing tongue, his huge mouth gaping wide and flaming, his blazing hair standing on end, tawny-eyed, he drank the fat of living creatures.
t.1.219.35: Then Madhusūdana saw the asura named Maya suddenly fleeing from the dwelling of Takṣaka.
t.1.219.37: Seeing the discus raised and the Fire, the Eater of Oblations, eager to burn him, Maya cried out, "Run to me, Arjuna!" O Bhārata.
t.1.219.36: Agni, whose charioteer is the wind, eager to burn him, went after him, having taken on a body with matted locks and roaring like a rain-cloud; and Vāsudeva, wishing to slay him, stood ready with his discus raised.
t.1.219.40: While that forest was burning, Agni did not burn six: Aśvasena, Maya, and the four Śārṅgakas.
t.1.219.38: Hearing his terrified cry, Dhanaṃjaya Pārtha replied to Maya, "Do not be afraid!", as if restoring him to life, O Bhārata.
t.1.219.39: When Pārtha had granted him safety, the Dāśārha did not wish to slay Maya, the brother of Namuci, and Pāvaka did not burn him either.
